lesson.title: Reading Inverse Slopes Off a Graph
lesson.summary: Because the graph of f^{-1} is the reflection of the graph of f across the line y = x, a tangent slope m at a point on f becomes a tangent slope 1/m at the reflected point on f^{-1}.
lesson.body:
The graph of f^{-1} is the reflection of the graph of f across the line y = x: every point (a, b) on f corresponds to a point (b, a) on f^{-1} (prerequisite: graphing functions). Reflecting across y = x swaps the roles of horizontal and vertical, so it swaps rise and run too, and a slope is nothing more than rise over run. That is the geometric reason the slope at the reflected point becomes the reciprocal: if the tangent line to f at (a, b) rises m units for every 1 unit across, then after reflection that same line rises 1 unit for every m units across, which is a slope of 1/m.

Make this concrete with f(x) = x^3 + 1. Since f(1) = 1^3 + 1 = 2, the point (1, 2) lies on the graph of f. Its derivative is f'(x) = 3x^2, so f'(1) = 3, meaning the tangent line at (1, 2) climbs with slope 3. Reflecting (1, 2) across y = x gives the point (2, 1), which lies on the graph of f^{-1}, and the reasoning above predicts the tangent slope there is the reciprocal, 1/3.

Because this f happens to be easy to invert, you can confirm the graphical reasoning with algebra. Solving y = x^3 + 1 for x gives f^{-1}(x) = (x - 1)^{1/3}, with derivative (1/3)(x - 1)^{-2/3}. At x = 2, (x - 1) = 1, so the derivative is (1/3)(1) = 1/3, exactly what the reflection argument predicted.

Two extra graphical facts fall out of this same picture. First, if f is increasing everywhere, its slopes are always positive, and the reciprocal of a positive number is still positive, so f^{-1} is increasing too. Second, wherever f has a horizontal tangent, slope 0, the reflected point on f^{-1} would need a slope of 1/0, undefined, which shows up on the graph as a vertical tangent line. This is the same restriction the Inverse Function Theorem states algebraically as f'(a) not equal to 0, just visible directly from the picture instead.
